vignette:
The Weight of Glass and Silence

Margaret is a 48-year-old social ministry worker who has spent the better part of two decades helping others navigate the worst moments of their lives - domestic violence survivors, families in crisis, people who have lost everything. She is the kind of woman who knows how to sit with suffering. What she did not know, until fourteen months ago, was how to sit with her own.

On a Tuesday evening in early autumn, Margaret was driving home from a late shift at the community outreach center where she works. The road was familiar - one she had traveled hundreds of times - when a transport truck ran a red light at highway speed and struck the driver's side of her car. The vehicle spun, rolled, and came to rest against a concrete barrier. Margaret remembers the sound of the glass, the sudden and total silence that followed, and then the smell of something burning. She was certain, in those moments before the sirens arrived, that she was going to die alone on that road. She was trapped for nearly forty minutes before emergency crews were able to free her. She sustained a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, and lacerations across her left arm and neck. Physically, she was told, she was lucky.

The first weeks after the accident are something of a blur. Friends from her church congregation brought meals. Her supervisor arranged for extended leave. Margaret told everyone she was fine - a word she had heard trauma survivors use defensively for years, and one she now found herself reaching for automatically. She was not fine. She could not sleep for more than two or three hours at a stretch before waking in a full sweat, convinced she could hear the truck, convinced the silence was coming again. During the day, she moved through her apartment carefully, as though the floor might give way.

When she returned to work two months later, colleagues noticed she seemed different - quieter, more guarded. Margaret noticed it too. She found herself unable to sit through client intake interviews involving accidents or medical trauma without her chest tightening so severely that she had to excuse herself. She began rerouting her commute to avoid the intersection where the crash occurred, adding nearly twenty minutes to her drive each way. She stopped accepting evening shifts entirely. The woman who had once been the steadiest presence in any crisis room now flinched at the sound of a truck engine on the street outside.

At home, the evenings are the hardest. Margaret sits with the television on but rarely watches it - the noise is a kind of company, a way of filling the silence that has come to feel dangerous to her. She has stopped cooking elaborate meals, stopped calling her sister as often as she used to, stopped attending the Friday evening prayer group she had been part of for eleven years. She tells herself she will go back when she feels more like herself, though she is no longer entirely sure who that person was.

What troubles Margaret most - and what she speaks about with a kind of quiet bewilderment - is the guilt she carries about her own distress. She has sat across from people who have survived things she cannot imagine, and she listened to them without judgment. She believed them when they said they were not the same. Now she finds herself applying a different standard to her own pain, as though her suffering is somehow less legitimate, less earned. She knows, intellectually, that this is not true. She has said as much to clients. But knowing and feeling, she has discovered, are very different kinds of knowing.

Margaret comes to sessions dressed neatly, her manner composed and professional. She is thoughtful and articulate, and she often reflects on her own responses with the careful language of someone trained to observe human behavior. Underneath that composure, though, is a woman who is exhausted - from vigilance, from grief, from the effort of holding herself together in a life that no longer quite feels like hers.
